evidence.label: A sharp entropy bound and the simplex inequality for isotropic constants

headline: In every dimension, simplices alone have the largest isotropic constant among convex bodies, the paper claims.
scope: The result covers every convex body in every dimension, and every log-concave probability density for the entropy bound.
plain: The isotropic constant compares how spread out a random point of a solid shape is with the shape's volume. The strong isotropic constant conjecture says the simplex, such as a triangle or tetrahedron, gives the largest value. This paper claims to prove it in every dimension, with simplices as the only maximizers. It also claims a sharp lower bound on the entropy of log-concave distributions. No Lean formalization is listed.
doesNot: This does not add anything new to the dimension-free slicing bound, which Klartag and Lehec had already proved.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.significanceWhy: If the proof holds, it finds the exact extreme shape for a central quantity in convex geometry, in every dimension.

explanation:
Take three flat shapes: a square, a disk and a triangle. Drop a random point uniformly inside each. Measure how spread out that point is, using its covariance [the table of variances in each direction]. Then compare the spread with the area. The isotropic constant L packages this comparison into one number[2].

Here are the values, computed exactly. The square gets the square root of 1/12, about 0.2887. The disk gets 1/(2√π), about 0.2821. The triangle gets about 0.3102. The triangle wins. Stretching, turning or sliding a shape does not change its L[3]. So every triangle gets the same 0.3102.

The paper claims the triangle pattern holds in every dimension[1]. Among all convex bodies [solid shapes with no dents], simplices have the largest isotropic constant. A simplex is the higher-dimensional triangle, such as a tetrahedron in three dimensions. The paper also claims simplices are the only maximizers[4]. The simplex value is about 0.3102 in two dimensions and about 0.3225 in three.

The question goes back to the slicing problem, from Bourgain's 1986 work[5]. It asked whether L stays below one fixed number in every dimension. Klartag proved a bound growing like the fourth root of the dimension, in 2006[6]. Later work by many authors brought this down step by step. Klartag and Lehec then proved a bound independent of dimension, using Guan's estimate[7]. But a universal bound does not name the largest value or the shape that reaches it[8].

The exact answer was known only in the plane. There Campi, Colesanti and Gronchi proved the triangle bound, and Saroglou proved the triangle is the only maximizer[9]. In higher dimensions, Rademacher showed in 2016 that a maximizer with triangular faces must be a simplex[10]. That ruled out some shapes but not all.

The paper's route goes through entropy. The differential entropy of a distribution measures how spread out and unpredictable it is. A log-concave density is one whose logarithm is concave, so it has one hump. The paper claims every such density in m dimensions has entropy at least m plus half the log of its covariance determinant[11]. Equality holds only for stretched and shifted products of one-sided exponential laws[12].

Check it in one dimension. The exponential law with mean 1 has entropy 1 and variance 1. The bound is 1 + ½ log 1 = 1, so it is met exactly. The uniform law on [0, 1] has entropy 0 and variance 1/12. Its bound is 1 + ½ log(1/12), about −0.2425, which 0 clears. The bell curve has entropy about 1.419, well above 1.

Melbourne, Nayar and Roberto had proved this one-dimensional case[13]. Fradelizi and Marín Sola stated the general bound and showed it matches the simplex bound across dimensions[14]. So proving the entropy bound in every dimension gives the simplex result. The hard part is equality. The expected extreme cases have cut-off supports, so smooth approximations alone cannot capture them[15]. Part of the proof rests on explicit one-variable inequalities whose constants are exact fractions[16].

There is a further consequence. Klartag showed in 2018 that the sharp simplex bound implies a nonsymmetric Mahler inequality, on a shape's volume times its polar's volume[17]. In two dimensions that floor is 27/4 = 6.75. A square from −1 to 1 has area 4, and its polar diamond has area 2. Their product, 8, sits above the floor.

How sure is this? No Lean formalization is listed for this paper in the openai/math release. So no computer proof checker has checked it. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Major only if the proof holds. It claims the exact extreme shape in every dimension, building on the already-proved dimension-free bound. No Lean formalization is listed and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A bounded solid shape with no dents and a nonempty inside.
A number comparing the spread (covariance) of a uniform random point in a shape with the shape's volume.
The higher-dimensional version of a triangle: a segment, triangle, tetrahedron, and so on.
The table of variances and joint variations of a random point's coordinates.
A number measuring how spread out and unpredictable a continuous distribution is.
A probability density whose logarithm is concave, giving a single hump.
The set of directions y with x·y at most 1 for every point x of the shape.
